title: Polygons As Finite Geometry
notes: Open with the promise of the chapter: a polygon is simple enough to draw, but rich enough to support algorithms, invariants, and impossibility results. The visual sequence previews the lecture path from inside-outside decisions to triangulations, guards, dissections, and finally the three-dimensional obstruction.

title: A Polygon Replaces Ambiguous Pictures
notes: Stress that the boundary is a finite cyclic list of straight segments. That finite representation lets an algorithm ask crisp questions: is a query on the boundary, inside, or outside; which segments can be used as diagonals; and which vertices can see a point or a triangle.

title: Ray Crossing Is A Parity Test
notes: Use the horizontal ray as a computational version of the Jordan curve intuition. Crossings toggle the state from outside to inside or back again. Boundary and vertex hits require conventions, so the clean statement is: away from the boundary, parity gives a stable inside-outside classifier.

title: Diagonals Are Interior Chords
notes: A diagonal is not just any segment between nonadjacent vertices. It must stay inside the polygon except at its endpoints. This distinction is where nonconvexity first matters: one candidate chord can be legal while another visibly exits the region.

title: Ears Make Induction Visible
notes: The ear theorem turns triangulation from a global mystery into a local removal move. If a vertex has an interior diagonal between its neighbors, that triangle can be clipped away and the remaining boundary is a smaller polygon. Repeating this move produces a triangulation.

title: Every Triangulation Has The Same Ledger
notes: After triangulation, the numerical invariants no longer depend on the particular diagonal choices. The triangle count is n minus 2 and the diagonal count is n minus 3. Present these as a planar graph ledger, not as a property of one drawing.

title: Euler Explains The Counts
notes: Walk through the bookkeeping. There are n boundary edges, d diagonals, and t triangular faces inside the polygon. Counting triangle sides gives 3t equals n plus 2d, and Euler's formula for the disk gives the second equation. Solving yields t equals n minus 2 and d equals n minus 3.

title: Convex Polygons Reveal Catalan Growth
notes: In a convex polygon every noncrossing chord is legal, so the remaining difficulty is combinatorial. Choosing the triangle incident to a marked edge splits the polygon into independent smaller polygons. That split is exactly the Catalan recurrence.

title: Triangulations As Graphs
notes: Shift attention from the geometry of segments to the graph carried by the triangulation. Vertices are polygon corners and edges are boundary edges plus diagonals. This graph is maximal outerplanar, which is why local triangle information controls global guarding arguments.

title: Fisk Coloring Turns Triangles Into Guards
notes: Fisk's proof colors the triangulation graph with three colors so that every triangle receives all three colors. The smallest color class then has at most floor n over 3 vertices, and because every triangle has a vertex of that color, those guards see the whole polygon.

title: Why The Least Color Class Guards
notes: Make the visibility argument geometric. A triangulation partitions the polygon into triangles. A guard placed at a vertex of a triangle sees that triangle because triangles are convex. If every triangle has a selected-color vertex, the union of visible triangles is the whole polygon.

title: Guard Bounds Change With The Rules
notes: The art-gallery theorem is a template, not a single universal number. Orthogonal galleries, exterior fortress guarding, and visibility restrictions change the combinatorial object being covered. The slide is a comparison map: the proof strategy remains triangulate, color, and count, while the bound changes.

title: Area Is A Complete 2D Dissection Invariant
notes: Introduce scissors congruence in the plane as an optimistic result. Polygonal pieces can be cut and rearranged, and equal area is the only obstruction for polygonal regions. The teaching point is that triangulation reduces arbitrary polygons to pieces that can be compared through area-preserving rearrangements.

title: A Triangle Can Become A Rectangle
notes: Use the diagram as a proof roadmap rather than a recipe for physical cutting. A triangle can be decomposed into pieces that reassemble as a rectangle with the same base-height area. Once polygons have been triangulated, this move lets area bookkeeping drive dissection.

title: Equal Volume Is Not Enough In 3D
notes: The three-dimensional story breaks the plane analogy. Tetrahedral dissections preserve volume, but they also preserve an angle-weighted ledger now called a Dehn invariant. Two polyhedra can have equal volume and still fail this second test, so they cannot be scissors congruent.

title: Chapter 1 Invariants To Reuse
notes: Close by naming the reusable mental tools. Parity classifies points, ears drive induction, Euler counts triangulations, Catalan recurrence counts convex choices, three-coloring gives guards, area controls planar dissections, and Dehn-angle data blocks the naive three-dimensional extension.
